back: Uptime ÷ total time, vs successful requests ÷ valid requests. Request-based counts partial outages partially.
MTBF ÷ (MTBF + MTTR). Faster recovery is often the cheapest gain.

front: Three conditions for redundancy to work?
back: Spare capacity for the survivors, failure detection, and a way to shift work.
One spare beyond peak need; two spares (survive a failure during maintenance); a full duplicate.

front: Capacity to survive losing one of Z zones?
back: Each zone needs peak ÷ (Z − 1). Total: 2× peak for 2 zones, 1.5× for 3, 1.33× for 4.
One copy serves; a standby (hot, warm or cold) is promoted on failure. Simple writes, slower and rarely tested failover.
All copies serve; a failed one is removed from rotation. Proven daily, but needs headroom and, for data, conflict handling.

front: Why do apps stay broken after a DNS-based database failover?
back: They cache the old DNS answer or keep dead pooled connections.
One or more data centres with independent power and networking, within about 100 km of the region's other zones, single-digit ms apart.

front: Minimum NY–London round trip in fibre?
back: 2 × 5,600 km ÷ 200,000 km/s ≈ 56 ms; real routes are longer.

front: What does multi-region force on data?
back: Usually async replication (possible data loss on failover) and a write-ownership or conflict-resolution model.
Multiply: A1 × A2 × … × An. Always below the weakest link.
1 − (1 − A1)(1 − A2)…(1 − An), only if failures are independent.
Correlated failures: shared rack, AZ, build, dependency or config; failover machinery in series; overload cascades.
